I am not the first person to experience a silent retreat at the Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan. According to one duty manager there, that distinction goes to a group of tourists who rocked up a couple of years ago armed with notepads and pens, and scribbled to the staff that nobody was permitted to speak to them. I am, however, the first person to attend a silent retreat organised by the hotel itself. When the offer came in to test the programme, I laughed out loud for two minutes straight. Then I jumped at the chance. Like so many people, my nervous system is absolutely shot. My life is an unending chaos of demands and requests and notifications, most of which are presented to me as a matter of urgency. On my more masochistic days, I sometimes allow myself to count the seconds before somebody asks me for something. Rarely, if ever, do I make it to a hundred. The resort features one of the best hotels in the world Christian Horan So the thought of spending five days cut off from the world, in complete silence, sounded like the greatest luxury imaginable. Many silent retreats run a gamut of discomfort, from Vipassana (ten days of hardcore meditation and, from what I’ve heard, relentless sobbing) to three-day long Polish retreats spent in total darkness (crying levels unknown, but likely). However, this one takes place on a perfect island, in one of the best hotels on the planet. Your phone is taken from you upon arrival, White Lotus style . Your television will have already been removed from the wall. And, should you be tempted to sneak in a secret second device, the wifi router will be unscrewed and decommissioned. Buzzy Ubud, a frantic scramble of mopeds and humanity in that order, might only be minutes away geographically, but may as well be on a different planet for all you’ll see of it. Almost all of the experience will be spent in your room, a yoga dharma or the newly renovated Sacred River Spa. But this is fine; the room is colossal and has a private infinity pool, the dharma bright and airy, and the spa offering long and sumptuous treatments designed to leave you in a state of blissful grogginess. There are worse trade-offs, in other words. Luxury newsletter The inside track on tech, travel, philanthropy and the hottest handbags, cars and spas. Luxury newsletter Explore our newsletters Nevertheless, the shock of losing contact with the outside world (What if my kids get sick? What if I miss an important work request? What if the world blows up?) still left me in a minor state of anxiety. Phones, for better or worse, have become our touch point to the world. They’re how we communicate with others. They’re how we check the weather. They’re torches and clocks and stopwatches, and the things that our children force us to look up animal facts on. Relinquishing yours feels, at first, like losing a frontal lobe. Advertisement But this probably means that I needed time away from mine. And it’s with this spirit of adventure that I handed it over to Ibu Fera, the resort’s wellness mentor, to be safely kept in the hotel safe. Fera is the programme’s best possible advertisement. A former Buddhist nun, and a single mother, she manages to combine deep insight with irresistibly gossipy asides. Fera presented herself as my guardian angel and swiftly went about laying out the week’s itinerary. A yoga class at the resort At 6.30am every day there would be a one-on-one kundalini yoga class. My treatments would happen in the spa at 2pm, and a meditation session would take place at 5.30pm. Breakfast would be delivered to my room at 7am, lunch at 12pm and dinner at 7.30pm, all of which would be small and vegan. Buggies would escort me to each activity, to prevent me from wandering around yammering at people, and the in-room dining team had been strictly instructed to ignore any frantic, hungry demands for cheeseburgers. Top stories 1 Six unbeatable Cruise Month deals to book with Times Holidays now Promoted content Still, this left an awful lot of time by myself. And, despite the gorgeous room and beautiful surroundings — the windows looked out across the lush Ayung valley, alive with the sound of birds and insects and lizards — there really is nothing like a week alone to reinforce what terrible company you are. Fortunately, Fera and her team had supplied me with a book on meditation and an enormous painting by numbers canvas to keep me occupied during all this downtime. Heard about the cure for stress where you’re not allowed to speak? But the isolation was necessary. Fera said that we are all so busy in our day-to-day lives that our minds have become cloudy. Solitude and silence will clear them, and move us to a baseline of quiet peace. However, she was quick to warn me that I would soon start to notice unpleasant thoughts bubbling up. This, she said, is because it is easier to spot impurities in a clear glass of water. Advertisement And so it came to pass. As the days passed and my mind emptied, I began to experience all manner of low-level anxieties that I would normally drive away with a good old-fashioned doomscroll. In our meditation sessions, Fera taught me to become aware of these sensations as they emerged, to acknowledge them and let them pass. And, just like magic, they did. Vain or what? Celebrity 177 comments 5 Running on fumes: data shows England’s World Cup bid was doomed from start Football 138 comments Across our days Fera introduced me to a range of meditation techniques. Some were specific to the hotel — her Sacred Nap, which involves being suspended in a womblike hammock while she chants and rocks you to sleep like a baby — while others are easier to replicate at home. In particular, I find that the use of a mala (108 wooden beads in a loop that you pass through your fingers while repeating a mantra) is particularly effective at grounding me when I most need it. Guests take part in the Sacred Nap meditation technique KENSEET Meanwhile, the kundalini yoga sessions with my instructor Suwitra focused on fast, aggressive movements accompanied by short, powerful breaths that left me emotionally and physically exhausted. Throughout the week there was a sense that I was deliberately breaking down my old self — grouchy, put-upon, quick to react — so that I could replace him with something slower and more intentional. And I cannot overstate how much I needed this; on my second day, after a chakra alignment session, I was given a mild bollocking for being too stressed. However, the retreat worked. A reiki session late in my stay revealed that my mind had cleared considerably since arriving, although my body still clung on to a little residual tension. Inevitably, I found myself sobbing with gratitude during my last meeting with Fera. Maybe no amount of luxury can stop you crying during a silent retreat. Read more luxury reviews, advice and insights from our experts Advertisement All in all, the retreat left me feeling more tranquil and calm than I have been in as long as I can remember. That said, it’s easy to be tranquil in paradise, being served delicious food and never having to make a decision. In the cold, hard slog of reality, things wear off. My attempts to go vegan lasted a week on my return, because eventually I was ground down by my children constantly asking where all the sausages had gone. On caffeine and alcohol I’m doing much better, though. I’ve drunk booze exactly once in the hundred days or so since I’ve been back, and to my wife’s horror I’ve started to drink mugs of hot water instead of tea. Less successful has been my relationship to my phone, which is back to its previous absurd level. This is what I most need to remember about my time on the retreat: that things manage fine without me. On the morning of my sixth day, when Fera returned my phone, I realised that nothing bad had happened. The kids were OK. Only part of the world blew up. I didn’t need to be as plugged in as much as I was before, or as much as I have been since. Maybe I need to put my phone in a drawer soon to remind myself of this. A seven-day full-board Silent Retreat at Sayan costs $2,166pp, inclusive of airport transfers, spa treatments, yoga and meditation, and guidance from Ibu Fera. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets were scrambled after an aerial target entered Romanian airspace overnight. Romania’s Ministry of National Defence said its radar surveillance system detected the unidentified target manoeuvring near Chilia Veche, close to the river border, on Saturday night. The incident prompted the National Military Command Centre to alert emergency officials, with an RO-Alert warning sent to residents in northern Tulcea County at 11.32pm. Two F-18 aircraft from the Spanish Air and Space Forces, which were on Enhanced Air Policing duty, took off alongside an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter from the Romanian Air Force to monitor the situation. Radar signals then showed the aerial target entering Romanian national airspace near Chilia Veche, where the ministry said it followed “for a few minutes a route almost parallel to the Chilia arm”. The signal was then lost in the Pardina area and the alert ended at 12.48am. It comes just days after a Russian drone crashed in Solca , near the Ukraine border, after Putin's forces ramped up attacks with a fresh wave of drone and missile strikes on Kyiv earlier this week. Romania's Ministry of Defence said at the time the drone was in "national airspace" for around four minutes before falling near the town in Suceava County "without causing casualties or material damage". The incident prompted school closures in the area while both Romanian and Polish fighter jets scrambled to monitor the situation. On last night's mystery aerial target, the Ministry said in a post on X: "On the night of September 26, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defense detected an aerial target maneuvering in the area of the Chilia Veche locality, near the river border. " The National Military Command Center notified the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations regarding the implementation of population alert measures in the northern part of Tulcea County, and at 23:32, an RO-Alert message was transmitted. "Two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Forces, engaged in Enhanced Air Policing combat service, and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter of the Romanian Air Force, took off to monitor the situation. "According to radar signals, the aerial target entered national airspace near Chilia Veche, following for a few minutes a route almost parallel to the Chilia arm. The radar signal with the target was lost in the Pardina area. The air alert ended at 00:48."
